explanations.answer: He cheers for him as king
explanations.explanation: He sure does. Hushai, David's friend, walks up and says, “Long live the king! Long live the king!” He says it TWICE, friend. David had sent him back to the city for exactly this kind of moment (2 Samuel 15:32-34). I bet he figured two cheers beat one.

Not quite. Ahithophel is with Absalom in Jerusalem, but Hushai doesn't ask for him. The text has Hushai speak straight to Absalom, David's son, and he opens with “Long live the king! Long live the king!” He starts with a cheer, not a meeting request.

Hushai doesn't do quiet here. He speaks up right away and says, “Long live the king! Long live the king!” No silent bow, just a double cheer. Me? I'd go undercover and sweat through my apron before the first word came out, friend.

explanations.answer: Why he didn't go with David
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Absalom, David's son, asks Hushai, “Is this the loyalty you show your friend?” and then, “Why did you not go with your friend?” He's poking at Hushai's loyalty. That's a tough question to get when you've just walked in cheering.

explanations.answer: Why he came to the city so late
explanations.explanation: The text never has Absalom ask about timing. His question is about Hushai's friend: “Why did you not go with your friend?” Absalom, David's son, wants to know why Hushai stayed behind instead of leaving with David. Nothing in the passage says Hushai was late.

explanations.answer: Why he showed up without a gift
explanations.explanation: No gift talk here, friend. Absalom, David's son, asks Hushai about loyalty: “Is this the loyalty you show your friend?” Then he asks, “Why did you not go with your friend?” The question is about who Hushai stands with, not what he brought.

True. Hushai says, “As I served in your father’s presence, so also I will serve in yours.” He answers Absalom's question with a question of his own: “…whom should I serve if not his son?” I think that's a smooth answer.

It's true, actually. Hushai says to Absalom, “Furthermore, whom should I serve if not his son? As I served in your father’s presence, so also I will serve in yours.” He promises to serve Absalom the way he served David. That's his answer to Absalom's challenge.

Right. Ahithophel says that when all Israel hears Absalom has become a stench to his father, “…then the hands of all who are with you will be strengthened.” His advice is heavy, and I think this is a hard part of the story. But the text is clear about what he says it will do.

That's not what Ahithophel says. He says that once all Israel hears, “…the hands of all who are with you will be strengthened.” His focus is on Absalom's own supporters. The text says nothing about David returning.

The priests don't come up in Ahithophel's advice here. He says all Israel will hear that Absalom has become a stench to his father, and then “…the hands of all who are with you will be strengthened.” It's about boosting the people already with Absalom. Nothing is said about the priests.

explanations.answer: Like consulting the word of God
explanations.explanation: You got it. The writer says Ahithophel's advice “…was like the consultation of the word of God.” and both David and Absalom thought so. When your advice gets treated like that, you're a big deal. I can't even get a baker to trust my oven timer.

explanations.answer: Like the ruling of a judge
explanations.explanation: Close in feel, but that's not the comparison the text uses. It says Ahithophel's advice was “…like the consultation of the word of God.” Both David and Absalom held it in that kind of regard. That's some serious weight for one man's advice.

explanations.answer: Like the orders of a commander
explanations.explanation: Not that one, friend. The writer says Ahithophel's advice “…was like the consultation of the word of God.” David and Absalom both respected it that much. Nobody's treating it like an order from a commander.
It's false. Ahithophel isn't waiting around. He says, “Let me choose twelve thousand men and set out tonight in pursuit of David.” Tonight, friend. He doesn't want to wait even one night.

False is right. Ahithophel says, “Let me choose twelve thousand men and set out tonight in pursuit of David.” He's not waiting a few weeks, he's going TONIGHT. This man doesn't even want to sleep on it.
That's it. Ahithophel says, “I will strike down only the king” After he throws David into a panic and the people flee, that's his target. It's a plan aimed at one man.
No priests in this plan. Ahithophel says he'll throw David into a panic and all the people with him will flee, and then, “I will strike down only the king” The target is David.
Not the servants. Ahithophel says, “I will strike down only the king” The people with David are meant to flee, not to be struck down. The only man he names as his target is the king.

Yes. Ahithophel says, “You seek the life of only one man; then all the people will be at peace.” Absalom, David's son, is after one man's life, and Ahithophel claims the rest will settle down. It's a plan that sounds neat, and that's the scary part.

The opposite, actually. Ahithophel says, “You seek the life of only one man; then all the people will be at peace.” He's telling Absalom, David's son, that going after one man will calm everyone else. Peace is the promise, not war.
Not risk, friend. Ahithophel says, “You seek the life of only one man; then all the people will be at peace.” He's selling the plan as quick and calm for everyone else. The word he uses is peace.
It's false. The text says, “This proposal seemed good to Absalom and all the elders of Israel.” The elders like it too, not just Absalom. So the plan lands with both.

False is right. The text says, “This proposal seemed good to Absalom and all the elders of Israel.” Not just Absalom, but the elders too. When Absalom and the elders both like it, that's a pitch that landed.

It's false. Hushai says, “This time the advice of Ahithophel is not sound.” Those two words, “this time,” are doing a lot of work. Both David and Absalom held Ahithophel's advice in high regard (2 Samuel 16:23).

False is right. Hushai tells Absalom, “This time the advice of Ahithophel is not sound.” The text says Ahithophel's advice was “…like the consultation of the word of God.” (2 Samuel 16:23). I think pushing back on that takes nerve.
Right. Hushai says David “…is a man of war who will not spend the night with the troops.” So David isn't going to be sitting in a camp where he's easy to find. That's the argument Hushai is making.

Not the priests. Hushai says David “…is a man of war who will not spend the night with the troops.” The priests Zadok and Abiathar show up later in the passage, but not here. The point is that David won't be camped with his soldiers.
Close, but it's not servants. Hushai says David “…is a man of war who will not spend the night with the troops.” He's telling Absalom that David won't be easy to find. Servants don't come into it.
True. Hushai says, “Surely by now he is hiding in a cave or some other location.” He opens with “Surely,” and he doesn't hedge. That's a bold way to make an argument.
It's true, friend. Hushai says, “Surely by now he is hiding in a cave or some other location.” That's part of his argument that David won't be easy to find. And he says it with total confidence.

That's the word. Hushai says whoever hears will say, “There has been a slaughter among the troops who follow Absalom.” It's a hard picture. He's describing what the news would be if some of Absalom's troops fall first.

Not victory. Hushai says people would say, “There has been a slaughter among the troops who follow Absalom.” He's picturing bad news spreading, not good. That's the news he describes if some troops fall first.

Not surrender, friend. Hushai says whoever hears will say, “There has been a slaughter among the troops who follow Absalom.” The word is slaughter. He's describing what people would say if some of the troops fall first.

Yes. Hushai says, “I advise that all Israel from Dan to Beersheba... be gathered to you, and that you yourself lead them into battle.” Look at that, he puts Absalom, David's son, right at the front. It's a flattering plan, and Absalom likes it.

Not Ahithophel. Hushai says to Absalom, “…that you yourself lead them into battle.” Ahithophel had offered to pick twelve thousand men himself, and Hushai's plan doesn't give him that role. In Hushai's version, Absalom leads.

Not Joab. Joab was David's army commander (2 Samuel 8:16), but Hushai never mentions him in this plan. He tells Absalom, David's son, “…that you yourself lead them into battle.” The leader in this plan is Absalom.

True. Hushai says, “If he retreats to a city, all Israel will bring ropes to that city, and we will drag it down to the valley until not even a pebble can be found there.” That's a big speech. He's going all in.

It's true, actually. Hushai says that if David retreats to a city, “…all Israel will bring ropes to that city, and we will drag it down to the valley until not even a pebble can be found there.” He's painting a huge picture for Absalom. This is how he sells it.

That's right. Absalom and all the men of Israel say, “The advice of Hushai the Archite is better than that of Ahithophel.” David's friend wins the room. And remember, they started out liking Ahithophel's plan (2 Samuel 17:4).

It's the other way around. The men say, “The advice of Hushai the Archite is better than that of Ahithophel.” Ahithophel gave the first plan, and Absalom and the elders liked it (2 Samuel 17:4). But after hearing Hushai, they say his advice is better.
Not Zadok. Zadok is one of the priests Hushai goes to later (2 Samuel 17:15). The men say, “The advice of Hushai the Archite is better than that of Ahithophel.” Zadok isn't part of that vote.

explanations.answer: The LORD planned to defeat it
explanations.explanation: You got it. The text says, “For the LORD had purposed to thwart the good counsel of Ahithophel in order to bring disaster on Absalom.” Ahithophel's counsel was good, and the LORD purposed to thwart it. That's the real story behind the room.

The text doesn't say that. It says the elders liked Ahithophel's plan at first (2 Samuel 17:4). The reason given for the turn is this: “…the LORD had purposed to thwart the good counsel of Ahithophel in order to bring disaster on Absalom.”

That's not in the text. The writer gives the reason: “…the LORD had purposed to thwart the good counsel of Ahithophel in order to bring disaster on Absalom.” And Ahithophel's counsel was called good. This was the LORD's purpose at work.

explanations.answer: Cross over and don't stay the night
explanations.explanation: Yes. Hushai says, “Do not spend the night at the fords of the wilderness, but be sure to cross over.” He adds that otherwise the king and all the people with him “…will be swallowed up.” He tells them to move QUICKLY.

explanations.answer: Hide in a cave and wait it out
explanations.explanation: Not quite. Hushai did tell Absalom, “Surely by now he is hiding in a cave or some other location.” But that was part of his speech to Absalom. The message to David is, “Do not spend the night at the fords of the wilderness, but be sure to cross over.” Waiting isn't the plan.

explanations.answer: Come back and fight Absalom now
explanations.explanation: No, friend. The message is, “Do not spend the night at the fords of the wilderness, but be sure to cross over.” Hushai says otherwise the king and all the people with him “…will be swallowed up.” It's a message to get moving, not to start a fight.

True, friend. The text says, “But a young man did see them and told Absalom.” Jonathan and Ahimaaz “…dared not be seen entering the city.” Somebody saw them anyway. Their quiet job just got a lot less quiet.
It's true, friend. The text says, “…a young man did see them and told Absalom.” Jonathan and Ahimaaz had been careful not to be seen. Somebody spotted them anyway.
Yes. The man in Bahurim “…had a well in his courtyard, and they climbed down into it.” A well is a bold hiding place. I respect anybody willing to climb down into one.

Not a storeroom. The man in Bahurim “…had a well in his courtyard, and they climbed down into it.” Jonathan and Ahimaaz went down a well, not into a room. I'd have picked the storeroom myself, friend.

Not a stable, friend. The man in Bahurim “…had a well in his courtyard, and they climbed down into it.” The text puts them down a well, not in a stable. I'd have been too nervous to climb down there myself.

explanations.answer: She covers it and scatters grain on top
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The man's wife “…took a covering, spread it over the mouth of the well, and scattered grain over it so nobody would know a thing.” Cover first, then grain on top. I think that's quick thinking.

explanations.answer: She rolls a heavy stone over it
explanations.explanation: No stone in this story. The wife “…took a covering, spread it over the mouth of the well, and scattered grain over it so nobody would know a thing.” She didn't seal it, she disguised it. Grain on a cover looks like nothing at all.

explanations.answer: She stacks firewood all around it
explanations.explanation: Not firewood, friend. The text says the wife “…took a covering, spread it over the mouth of the well, and scattered grain over it so nobody would know a thing.” It's a cover with grain on top. A stack of firewood would probably get searched.
Right. She tells Absalom's servants, “They have crossed over the brook…” Meanwhile the two men are down in the well. The servants search but do not find them.
Not that one. The woman tells Absalom's servants, “They have crossed over the brook…” The servants do return to Jerusalem, but that's where they go after searching. Her answer is about the brook.
That's not what she says. Her answer is, “They have crossed over the brook…” She says nothing about never seeing them. She talks about the brook, while the men are down in the well.
It's false. The text says, “The men searched but did not find them, so they returned to Jerusalem.” Jonathan and Ahimaaz stayed hidden. The covering and the grain did their job.
False is right. “The men searched but did not find them, so they returned to Jerusalem.” They looked, and they came up empty. Two men down a well, and the servants went back to Jerusalem.
That's it, baker. “By daybreak, there was no one left who had not crossed the Jordan.” David and all the people with him got across. Not one person was left on the wrong side.
Not midnight. The text says, “By daybreak, there was no one left who had not crossed the Jordan.” Daybreak is the mark the text gives. By then David and all the people with him were across.

Not noon, friend. The text says, “By daybreak, there was no one left who had not crossed the Jordan.” Noon never shows up in the passage. The mark is daybreak, and by then David and all the people with him were across.

Yes, friend. Ahithophel “…saddled his donkey and set out for his house in his hometown.” He doesn't go back to Absalom, and he doesn't go to David. This is a heavy part of the story. I think this one hurts.

Not back to Absalom. The text says Ahithophel “…saddled his donkey and set out for his house in his hometown.” He leaves Absalom's side after his advice isn't followed. I think this is a hard moment for him.
Not David's camp. Ahithophel “…saddled his donkey and set out for his house in his hometown.” The text sends him home. And what he does there is a heavy part of the story.
